title: The 5 Deadliest Pandemics in History, Ranked (1918 Flu Is Only #2)

scenes.text: The 1918 flu killed at least 50 million people. It's only number two.
Number five: COVID-19. About 15 million extra deaths in its first two years alone, the WHO estimates.
scenes.label: COVID-19 · ~15M

scenes.text: Number four: HIV and AIDS. About 44 million lives since the 1980s, and the count is still rising.
scenes.label: HIV/AIDS · ~44M

scenes.text: Number three: the Plague of Justinian, in the year 541. Estimates run from 25 to 100 million.
scenes.label: Plague of Justinian · 25-100M

scenes.text: Number two: the 1918 flu. It infected about one in three people alive.
scenes.label: 1918 flu · 50-100M

scenes.text: Number one: the Black Death. Europe alone lost up to 50 million people, up to half of everyone, before counting Asia and Africa.
scenes.label: Black Death · 50M+ in Europe

description:
History's five deadliest pandemics by estimated deaths. Old tolls are rough and the ranges overlap, so this follows mainstream estimates: Gavi's list of history's deadliest plagues, plus CDC, WHO, UNAIDS and Britannica figures.
COVID-19: WHO estimates 14.9 million excess deaths in 2020-2021. HIV/AIDS: 44.2 million deaths since the epidemic began (UNAIDS, range 33.8-61.1 million). Plague of Justinian (from 541): 25-100 million (Britannica; Gavi 30-50 million). 1918 flu: at least 50 million (CDC), up to 100 million; about a third of the world was infected. Black Death (1347-1352): about 25-50 million in Europe, 30-60% of its people; Gavi's worldwide estimate is 75-200 million. Smallpox in the Americas is left out because its toll can't be separated from war and famine.
Which of these surprised you most?
first_comment: Estimates for the oldest ones vary a lot. Which would you put at number one, and what should we rank next?
